coach_says: Look at what White has left undefended before you start a fight: the c4 pawn had no protector at all (the bishop went to g2 and the d-pawn hasn't moved), so 6...Bxc4 just wins a pawn. Instead 6...d5 opens the centre while your king is still on e8 and your kingside pieces are undeveloped; after exd5 cxd5 d4 your centre pawns get attacked from every side. Before a pawn break, check for free material and make sure your king is ready for an open centre.
concept: missed the free pawn on c4
also: opened the centre with king uncastled

coach_says: Your e5 pawn was doing an important job: it blocked the diagonal from c7 to your rook on f4 and your h2 pawn, where Black's knight on g4 is already aiming. After 13.e6 Black plays ...Qc7, attacking the rook on f4, and if the rook moves away Qxh2+ comes; ...g5 next wins the exchange. Before pushing a pawn, ask what lines it opens toward your own king; 13.d3 developing the bishop was the calm choice.
concept: pawn push opened the diagonal to h2

coach_says: Your knight on e7 was attacked by the rook on e1 and its only defender was your king. Castling queenside moved the king away, so Rxe7 simply wins a knight. When a piece is pinned or guarded only by the king, check that it stays protected before you castle; 17...Kd8 or 17...Kf8 keeps the knight defended.
concept: castled away from the knight's only defender

coach_says: White's d-pawn is a passed pawn and your back rank is weak, so you must not let it advance with gain of time. 26...Nc6 puts the knight right where d5 attacks it, then d6 and Rc8+ come with your king stuck on g8. Keep pieces off squares where the passed pawn can hit them, and give your king a role: 26...Kf8 heads toward the pawn and covers the back rank.
concept: let their passed pawn advance with tempo

coach_says: On b4 your knight is attacked by the queen on d2 and defended only by the bishop on c5. White trades on e7 and plays d4, hitting that bishop, so the knight loses its protector and you drop a piece. When you move a piece to a square guarded only once, ask whether a pawn can chase the guard away; 11...Nd4 puts the knight on a strong square supported by the e5 pawn and the bishop.
concept: knight on b4 lost its only defender

coach_says: In this rook ending your a6 pawn is already attacked by the rook on c6, so a quiet king move just lets White take it and erase your extra pawn. 27...Re8 counterattacks the loose e4 pawn: after e5 dxe5 dxe5 Rxe5 your rook is active and you stay a pawn up. In rook endings, an active rook that attacks pawns is usually worth more than a careful king move.
concept: activate the rook against e4

coach_says: The knight on c7 forks your king and rook, but you can fight back: 15...Kd7 attacks the knight, so White has to take on a8 at once, then ...Bxa1 wins the other rook and your h8 rook can recapture on a8, leaving you a piece up. 15...Ke7 does not touch the knight, so White first saves the a1 rook with Rab1, hitting your bishop on b2, and only then takes on a8. When forked, look for a king move that attacks the forking piece.
concept: attack the forking knight with the king
also: move the king off the back rank so the rook can recapture

coach_says: Your king on f2 sits on the diagonal from a7 and Black is ready to check with ...Qb6+. The knight on e2 was the piece that supports d4, the pawn you need to block that check; 26.Nf4 walks away from that job and onto a square the h6 bishop can take. After ...Qb6+ d4 Rxe1 and ...Bxf4, the d4 pawn falls and Black's queen invades your exposed king. Ask what your opponent threatens before moving a defender away from your king.
concept: moved the king's defender away

coach_says: Your bishop on g4 does not really pin the knight: the bishop on e2 is behind it, not the queen, so the knight is free to move. After 4...e5 the knight takes on e5, which also uncovers the e2 bishop onto your g4 bishop, and you are simply a pawn down. Check what defends a pawn before you push it; 4...Bxf3 removes the knight that attacks both d4 and e5.
concept: pawn on e5 left undefended

coach_says: Your king on h1 is boxed in by Black's pawn on h2 and queen on h3, and Black's knight is one jump from f3. After 25.f5 Black plays ...Nf3 and then ...Qg4 and ...Qg1+ Rxg1 hxg1=Q mate. When your king is in a net like this, defence comes first: 25.f3 takes the f3 square from the knight and covers g4.
concept: ignored the mating threat around h1

coach_says: The g-file is open, White has a bishop on h6 and a rook ready for g1, and your king is on g8. 13...b5 ignores that: Rg1+ Kh8 Bg7+ Kg8 Bxf6+ leads to mate or wins your queen. Before starting play on the queenside, step off the open file: 13...Kh8 lets you meet Rg1 with ...Rg8.
concept: king left on the open g-file

coach_says: Black's queen and the pawn on h2 already trap your king, and the knight on d4 is the piece that finishes the job by jumping to f3. 24.Bxd4 removes that attacker, and you stay better. After 24.cxd6 the knight lands on f3 and Black mates or wins heavy material. When your king is under attack, trade off the attacking pieces before going after material.
concept: trade off the attacking knight

coach_says: You are a piece down, so you need activity, not retreats. 23.Be3 is passive and lets Black play ...e5, develop the knight and castle. 23.Rfe1 attacks the queen with tempo and puts a rook on the e-file against the king still on e8. When behind, look for moves that attack something and keep the enemy king in the centre.
concept: keep pieces active when behind
also: rook to the open file with tempo

coach_says: Choose the capture that leaves you something extra. 12.Bxc4 dxc4 Nxc4 wins Black's c4 pawn back for free, and that knight can then jump to d6 with check if Black grabs d4. After 12.Nxc4 dxc4 you cannot take back with the bishop, because ...Qxd4 hits the bishop and b2. You are still winning, but you gave up an easy pawn.
concept: capture with the right piece

coach_says: Your knight on f6 is blocking your g7 bishop, which aims straight at the d4 knight, the undefended c3 knight and the a1 rook. 13...Nfd5 moves the knight with a threat on c3 and opens the bishop's diagonal at the same time, so White's knights are in trouble. Castling is safe but slow, and it gives White time for Bb2. When a piece blocks your bishop's long diagonal, look for a move that clears it with a threat.
concept: clear the bishop's long diagonal

coach_says: Both recaptures are fine, but think about which file each one opens. 10.hxg3 opens the h-file for your rook on h1, and with the bishop on d3 also hitting h7 you win that pawn straight away. 10.fxg3 opens the f-file instead, which gives you nothing immediate. When choosing how to take back with a pawn, check which file opens and whether your rook can use it.
concept: recapture to open the h-file

coach_says: You are a piece down, and White's queen on g5 is out on its own. 11...h6 and then ...g5 chase it with pawns until it runs short of squares; if it takes on h6, ...Ng4+ forks king and queen. That forces White to give material back. 11...Bb4 is a slow move that lets White play Bd3 and stay a piece up. When the enemy queen wanders forward, kick it with pawns and count its escape squares.
concept: chase the exposed queen with pawns

coach_says: Black's bishop on c5 points at g1 and your king is still in the centre, while your kingside pieces sit at home. 10.d4 takes the centre and hits that bishop with gain of time. 10.Bc3 moves an already developed piece to a square where it does little. Early on, play central pawn moves that blunt your opponent's best bishop and develop the rest of your pieces.
concept: strike the centre with d4
also: blunt the bishop aimed at your king

coach_says: Take back towards the centre: 13...bxc6 keeps a pawn covering d5, so White's knight can never settle there, and it opens the b-file against White's king on c1. After 13...Bxc6 the d5 square is a permanent home for White's knight, because no black pawn can kick it. When choosing a recapture, think about which squares your pawns will control afterwards.
concept: recapture with the pawn to control d5
also: open the b-file against the king

coach_says: In this sharp line the key is to hit White's king first: 5...Bxf2+ drags the king out, and after Kxf2 Nxe4+ you get a strong attack that balances the material. 5...Qe7 is too slow, White takes the h8 rook and you are just an exchange down. In gambit positions, use checks while the king is exposed, before your opponent can grab material and get organised.
concept: check the king first with Bxf2+
